chapter_theme: The fifth ten, Paranar's songs for Kadal Pirakkottiya Senguttuvan: the bard's hard road to the king whose feet toiled at sea, scarred warriors and horses beyond counting, gifts like drought-breaking rain, the war at Mohur for a distant kinsman and the neem made into a drum, a king without equal who drove back the sea, performers who never take their leave, slaughter that is itself a gift, a name to outlast the river sands, a virali guided by the Mohur slaughter, and the sleepless king in camp; the preface adds the northern expedition for the Pattini stone and the Chola wars.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet has crossed the dry road to see the king and praises him on sight

41.reading: The poet tells how his band of young performers, carrying lute, drums and horns packed in their bundles and praising the god, crossed many dry tracks of a forest where rain has failed and the bamboo withers, where a mighty elephant, taking a sound for the roar of a tiger pack, tears down a branch of flame-flowered vengai and wears it on its head like warriors of the army meeting battle, staff in hand; he has come to see the faultless lord of the strong chariot, and he asks whether the king's feet, which rode the swift maned horse and toiled in the cold sea of crashing waves, can be free of weariness, the feet of a king whose one-word warriors fulfilled their vows, broke kings in drum-loud battle and pounded enemy heads as pestles pound pepper.
41.nuance: The poem is in two halves: the hardship of the road the poet bore to see the king, and then the hardship the king's own feet bore at sea, so the bard's journey and the king's campaign are set against each other. The question தாவல் உய்யுமோ (line 17) is a turn of courtesy, concern for the king's feet, that becomes praise of the campaign. The elephant that mistakes something for a tiger and attacks the vengai rests on the old pairing of the vengai's flowers with the tiger's stripes.

comparisons.vehicle: செல்படை மறவர் தண்(டு)உடை வலத்தர் போர்எதிர்ந் தாங்கு
comparisons.tenor: the elephant wearing the torn vengai branch and trumpeting

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's warriors and of his gifts of horses

42.reading: The poet hails Kuttuvan, husband of the fair-browed queen and lord of men who wear the dark palmyra garland and anklets of giving, whose chests are deeply scarred where the long white needle went in and out like a kingfisher diving into a cold pool for fish and rising again, and who wear the thumbai only beside men whose bodies have taken arrows; after each battle won he puts on a fresh garland strewn with inji flowers, pours sweet gem-coloured wine from sandal-smeared jars with unsparing joy so that the great kin of the performers thrive, and the prancing maned horses he has showered on them, if counted, are more than the cold waves of the dark clear sea that come crashing in white-crested spray.
42.nuance: The scar is the warrior's credential: thumbai is worn only with those already wounded, so courage is counted on the body before the gift is counted in horses. The kingfisher simile is of the surgeon's needle sewing the wound, the bird's dive and rise matching the needle's passage through the flesh.

comparisons.vehicle: மீன்தேர் கொட்பின் பனிக்கயம் மூழ்கிச் சிரல்பெயர்ந் தன்ன
comparisons.tenor: the long needle passing in and out of the warriors' wounds
the horses the king has given

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's conquests and of his giving to every kind of suppliant

43.reading: The poet hails Kuttuvan of the gold garland, whose slaying army broke in shouting battle the drum-rich kings between the Himalaya, the god-haunted high mountain of the north where women with chowrie tufts swing and the musth tuskers come with she-elephants beyond counting, and Kumari in the south, and spoiled the old beauty of lands of many tongues; as in a drought, when palmyras wither, hills go dry and falls stop, the roaring sky pours rain with thunder and breaks the banks of the great river while ploughmen wearing konrai yoke their ploughs, so he lets the ascetics eat their fill, scatters jewels to the merry, and bids that the singing viralis get many she-elephants, the plundering warriors get killing tuskers and the herald who praises the field get horses; since he loves war, even his foes praise him, and the poet has seen his state at feasts where the fat-smoke fire never dies and the toddy never fails the musicians.
43.nuance: The rain is not the ordinary rain of the season but rain that breaks a drought, so the king's gift is measured against need, not against plenty. The roll of gifts is graded by receiver: she-elephants to the singing women, war tuskers to the fighters, horses to the herald, each gift fitted to its use.

comparisons.tenor: the king's giving to every suppliant

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's giving and of his war at Mohur

44.reading: The poet hails the lord of swaying gait whose victorious banner touches the sky on his chariot amid a roar like the earth being struck, who flings away unsparingly what he won in battle without calling it rare, and has never known even in dream to say 'hold back': for the sake of Arukai of the fine uzhinai, whom he called kin though far off and who had fled his land in an unended feud, he stormed the fort like one possessed, took the drum of the king of Mohur, humbled his boast, cut down his neem at the root, yoked many elephants to drag it for a drum, on the Kuraalam field where tufted owls cry and the crossroads grieve; he drove off many drum-rich kings, and his land is the one where the vanni common holds the urns that hid kings who once ruled the wide earth.
44.nuance: The war is told as a friend's duty: the king fights Mohur because Arukai, distant though he is, was declared kin (சேணன் ஆயினும் கேள்என மொழிந்து). The felled guardian neem becomes the victor's own war drum, so the enemy's sacred tree is made to sound his victories. Line 8, காணிலியரோ, and the burial urns of the last lines are hard to construe.

comparisons.tenor: the roar of the king's army

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king as without equal among kings past and present

45.reading: The poet asks whether there are now, or were before, any kings like this Cheral, who wears the gold thumbai and the chest-garland won from seven crowns, whose arrows lie quiet in the spotted quiver like snakes in an anthill, whose bow bends and heart does not, whose spears are notched from striking elephants; who crossed the deep-moated walls of forts that others had sacked and enjoyed of old, raised his land-winning shoulders like the bars that guard a gate, danced the thunangai on the corpse-heaped field, fed meat-paste rice to men who never retreat, and threw his spear to drive back the roaring cold sea that rain clouds do not empty nor rivers fill.
45.nuance: The sea that neither shrinks when clouds drink from it nor swells when rivers enter (lines 19, 20) is the image of what cannot be moved, and the king moves it; the sea-repelling feat that gives the decade's king his name is here the climax of a list of land battles. The question 'are there such now? none before you either' makes the praise historical: he is measured against all past kings.

comparisons.tenor: the arrows resting in the quiver

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king whose bounty keeps the performers from leaving

46.reading: Because Kuttuvan of victorious fame, lord of killing elephants who crossed many battles cutting countless heads, whose chariot wheel runs over many wastes, and who threw his spear to drive back the conch-loud sea of breaking waves, protects them well and pours sweet joy on them, the women in jewels, ear-rings and cool garlands, with bright bangles and gem-lit breasts and bee-haunted hair, tune the great lute to the paalai mode and sing the uzhinai of his unbowing line; those who have seen him never say 'we will go', and move about only singing.
46.nuance: The praise works by an absence: the performers never speak the word of leave-taking (செல்குவம் என்னார்), which in other gift poems is the moment the bard departs rewarded. The women sing a war theme, uzhinai, in the paalai mode of the lute, a music named for the parting land.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's slaying and of the suppliants' unending gain

47.reading: Kuttuvan never tires of slaying, and each time he slays the suppliants never tire of receiving elephants; and in his ancient city, where banners wave in the wind from the mansions like falls pouring down a mountain, where the big lamps on their stands burn with broad flames fed from ghee-dripping spouts, and bright-browed viralis dance, the talk of him never ends.
47.nuance: The eight lines are built on one verb repeated three times, ஆனான், ஆனார், ஆனா: the king's killing, the suppliants' gain and the city's talk of him are made one unbroken chain, so that each slaughter is at once a gift.

comparisons.tenor: the banners rippling from the mansions

thinai_evidence.note: the king's nature is told and his name blessed

48.reading: The poet blesses the name of the king who crowns the bards with gold lotuses and hangs necklaces on the bright-browed viralis, who set his imperishable fame by entering the water and toiling with the sea, lord of the paravar of the cold shore, of whom his skilled attendants say as they stand in rows that he gives here easily, even to songs that ask nothing, the treasure he took there at sea, a man of truth who never learned otherwise; gentle in bearing and unbending in manhood, his many-spotted chest has lost its garland and sandal to the fire that burns the enemy front; may his name live longer than the sands of the great Kaanchi ford where bands bathe in the sweet water born on his mountains and rushing to his sea, at the festival where kin enjoy a summer life in the groves.
48.nuance: The king is addressed as lord of the fishermen (பனித்துறைப் பரதவ) because of his sea war, and the river that runs from his mountain to his sea makes the whole land, hill to shore, his. வணங்கிய சாயல் வணங்கா ஆண்மை (line 9) pairs a bowing gentleness with an unbowing manhood; the line recurs in 70. Whether காஞ்சி names a river or the kaanchi trees of the ford is not settled by the poem.

comparisons.tenor: the years the king's name should live

thinai_evidence.note: a performer guides the viralis to the king

49.reading: The speaker calls the viralis of swaying gait and drooping garlands to come along with him so that their kin who live by song may eat well, for he has seen Kuttuvan of great anger, who, when kings and Velir agreed together and came crowding to Mohur swollen with strength, with elephants spreading, horses held in, banners gleaming and chariots wheeling, charged so that the massed array shook, while red-handed warriors' blood ran over the ground like a rain-day flood filling the hollows, corpses heaped up, the drum roared in the middle, the place was ruined and many dwellers died, and he cut down the victorious neem of dark branches.
49.nuance: The guide does not describe the gifts at all, only the slaughter at Mohur: the proof that the viralis will eat well is the scale of the king's victory. The blood-flood simile borrows the rain image of plenty for the field of the dead.

comparisons.tenor: the blood running over the battlefield

thinai_evidence.note: the king is on campaign in the war camp, taking the enemy's country

50.reading: The poet tells the king that he is like the confluence where the Kaveri, flowing due east in muddy flood and fed by rains that thunder like mountains, scatter hail and make the deer herds tremble, enrich the cane-fields and sustain the world, joins two more flowery streams; having crossed battles at forts on hills and by the sea, taken the enemy's land and filled his foes with dread, he asks how the many days pass for the great one whose eyes, in the camp where hatred of the enemy keeps him, cannot even take a short hard-won sleep and are woken by the roar of horns, when he might lie embraced on the soft pillow of women's loosened hair, their sandal and colour rubbed away and bees humming on their breasts.
50.nuance: The poem praises endurance by naming what the king gives up: the embrace is drawn in akam detail and then set aside for the camp's broken sleep, so the king's love is the measure of his resolve. Lines 8 to 10 are partly corrupt (மன்ண, வொணஇய), and the sense of the army as a flood that is the kings' fortress is a guess.

thinai_evidence.note: the preface tells the northern expedition and the wars that followed

patikam:5.reading: The decade's preface says that Senguttuvan, who drove back the sea, son of Nedum Cheralathan, lord of the westerners whose sky-touching banner the northerners fear, by the Chola Manakkilli, went through the forests by the arrow to take a stone for the goddess Pattini, defeated the Aryan lord, bathed it in the far-famed Ganga of sweet falls, brought back herds of cows with their calves, camped outside Idumbil, cut down Viyalur where warriors like tigers fell, reached the far bank and destroyed Kodukur, felled the whole trunk of the dark neem guarded by Pazhaiyan, yoked it to an elephant cart with ropes of the hair of his many wives, who had put off their jewels, killed nine of the Chola line in endless battle, camped at their gate and broke their standing strength; and that Paranar of flawless verse sang this ten.
patikam:5.nuance: The preface tells what the songs leave out: the northern expedition for the Pattini stone and the Chola wars. It also names whose neem was felled (Pazhaiyan's) and the ropes that dragged it, the hair of his widowed wives, which the songs (44, 49) only touch on.

links.note: Kural 776 says the hero counts as wasted every day on which he took no noble wound; Patitruppattu 42 says the king's men wear the thumbai only beside men whose bodies already hold arrows and whose chests show the surgeon's needle-scars.
links.teaches: The Kural keeps the ledger of wounds inside one man's private reckoning, while the Chera poem turns it into a rule of the company, so that scars decide who may stand in the thumbai line and the wound becomes a public credential rather than a personal measure.

links.note: Kural 211 says duty seeks no return, as the world gives nothing back to the rain; Patitruppattu 43 likens the king's giving to rain that breaks a drought and floods the river banks.
links.teaches: Both take rain as the model of giving, but the Kural uses it to show giving without return, while the Chera poet uses drought-breaking rain to show giving measured by need and graded by receiver, so the same image yields a rule of disinterest in one and a rule of fit in the other.

links.note: Patitruppattu 11 says Nedum Cheralathan cut down the enemy's kadamba at the root and made of it his roaring war drum; Patitruppattu 44 says his son cut the Mohur king's neem at the root to make a drum and dragged it off with elephants.
links.teaches: Read together, the father's kadamba and the son's neem show the guardian tree turned into the victor's drum as a rite of the Chera line, repeated across generations, so that each king's voice in war is literally made from a defeated enemy's sacred tree.

links.note: Akananuru 347 measures the town's gossip by the drum of Cheralathan made from the kadamba he cut after driving back the sea; Patitruppattu 44 shows the making of such a drum from the Mohur neem.
links.teaches: The puram decade shows how a Chera trophy drum was made from a felled guardian tree, and the akam poem shows that drum so well known that a heroine can use its roar to measure the gossip about her, so a war trophy had passed into the household's common speech.

links.note: Patitruppattu 20 says Nedum Cheralathan went against foes on an island in the sea and cut their kadamba; Patitruppattu 45 says his son threw his spear and drove back the sea itself, which no rain or river can change.
links.teaches: Set side by side, the father's war against islanders in the sea and the son's spear thrown at the sea show the decade's title growing from a naval campaign into a feat against nature, with the human enemy dropped and the sea left as the only adversary worth naming.

links.note: Patitruppattu 47 says that whenever Kuttuvan slays, the suppliants never cease receiving elephants; in Purananuru 394 a bard given a killing elephant is terrified, sends it back, and is given a bigger one, so he warns other poets away.
links.teaches: On one reading the war elephant is the crown of royal gifts, and on the other it is a burden a poor bard cannot use or feed, so the pair shows the gift-poem's ideal of the elephant gift and the bard's comic protest against it from inside the same tradition.

links.note: Patitruppattu 44 gives the cause of the Mohur war, the king's pledge to the distant Arukai, and the felling of the neem; Patitruppattu 49 gives the kings and Velir who massed at Mohur, the blood-flood and the ruin.
links.teaches: The two songs divide one campaign between them, the reason and the trophy in one and the coalition and slaughter in the other, so the decade tells a single war across separate praise poems and needs both to be read as history.

links.note: Akananuru 214 has a soldier in the rain-soaked camp where the king, eager for glory, does not sleep, asking how his wife bears the evenings alone; Patitruppattu 50 asks how the sleepless king himself passes the camp days away from women's embrace.
links.teaches: The akam poem treats the king's sleeplessness as the cause of the soldier's separation, while the puram poet lends the king the soldier's own longing to praise his endurance, so the same camp night is a lover's grief in one book and a king's virtue in the other.

links.note: Patitruppattu 44 says the king cut the Mohur neem at the root and dragged it with elephants for a drum; the preface names it as the neem guarded by Pazhaiyan and says the elephant cart was tied with ropes of his widowed wives' hair.
links.teaches: The preface supplies the detail the song withholds, the rope of the defeated king's widows' hair, so the felling of the tree is shown to be a humiliation of the enemy's household as well as the taking of his sacred tree.

source_issues: 41-50: no poem colophon gives a thinai (all null); 50 is marked vanji for its war camp and the preface vanji for the northern expedition, the rest paadaan.
41: show flags a line after the colophon kept in colophon_raw, not verse. Line 11 சேஎர் is unclear (the Chera people, or சேர் 'reach').

42 line 9 தாணஇ and 50 lines 10, 23, 26 வொணஇய, மாணஇப், மாணஇய look like encoding leftovers (ணஇ for a long vowel sign); 50 line 9 மன்ண is probably a misprint for மின்ன (flashing). 50 line 8 has a stray comma inside the line.
42 line 21 and 46 line 11 spell பெளவம் with ெ + ள rather than the vowel sign ௌ.
44 line 8 காணிலியரோ and lines 18 and 22-23 are hard to construe; 44 line 1 துடையூ is unusual and may be corrupt.
Repaired lines (flags): 42 line 23, 43 line 4, 46 line 13, 48 line 10, 49 line 5 and patikam:5 line 6; all repaired readings are plausible.
48 line 9 (வணங்கிய சாயல் வணங்கா ஆண்மை) is repeated at 70 line 20, and 49 line 5 at 81 line 7 (flagged).
patikam:5 line 23 (காசறு செய்யுட் பரணர் பாடினார் பத்துப்பாட்டு.) is the prose colophon kept as a verse line.
